To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
most CIs are very useful for assessing replication but that there are a few that are not.

most 95% confidence intervals (CIs), when they are correct, will include 90% or so of future replication means, but a few will include much less than that, and the average 95% CI, when correct, includes 83% of replication means.
95% Cis will capture 83.4%, on average, of replication means and that 90% of 95% C is will capture 90% or less of replication means.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how well confidence intervals capture replication means, and how this information can be conveyed to researchers.
what CIs and p values can and cannot tell us about replication.
the question of how much information about replication is provided by confidence intervals and p values.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
95% Cis capture 95% of future replication values, but this statement is not helpful in understanding how CIs work.
a 95% confidence interval includes about 83% of replication means and about 5% of replication means are outside of the 95% CI.
95% Cis are expected to include 83.4 percent of the future replication means, with a 5 percent chance of including less.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
CIs and p values can give information about replication but that this information is limited and needs to be interpreted with caution.
the percentage of the replication means that a CI captures depends on where in relation, to the population mean the CI falls, but the average percentage is around 83%.
the percentage of replication means captured by 95% Cis is typically much higher than the percentage of replication results that would be statistically significant.
The main takeaway from our work is that
researchers should not be misled into thinking that a particular CI is likely to be a good predictor of where the next replication mean will fall.
CIs and p values are not the only information that researchers need to understand the replication problem.
CIs can be used to make inferences about replication.
